title: Claude Identity Verification API Integration: APAC KYC Guide
summary: Step-by-step Claude identity verification API integration for APAC fintech and e-commerce onboarding, with code, n8n orchestration, and MAS/HKMA compliance notes.
body_markdown:
**Quick Answer:** A Claude identity verification API integration uses Claude's vision and tool-use to extract structured fields from ID documents, then reconciles them against a licensed IDV vendor's biometric and sanctions results. Claude assists extraction; it does not make the KYC decision. Zero Data Retention is mandatory for regulated workloads.


---


A Singapore-licensed payments firm I spoke with last quarter had a very specific operational problem. Their onboarding queue for corporate accounts had a 38-hour median turnaround, and 70% of that time was a human analyst squinting at a scanned Hong Kong Business Registration certificate, a Companies Registry extract, and three director passports — then typing the fields into a case management tool. Their compliance team wasn't slow. They were doing data entry.


*Related reading:*[Headless Commerce Business Case Builder for APAC Teams](https://branch8.com/posts/headless-commerce-business-case-builder-apac)


That is the real use case behind a Claude identity verification API integration: not replacing your KYC vendor, but putting a document-understanding layer between the raw artefacts your customer uploads and the structured decision your compliance system needs. Claude reads the documents, extracts fields into a schema, flags mismatches, and writes an auditable rationale. A dedicated IDV provider still does the biometric match, liveness check, and sanctions screening. Those are two different jobs, and conflating them is how teams end up with a regulator asking uncomfortable questions.


*Related reading:*[Staff Augmentation vs Managed Squad: APAC Tech Decision Guide](https://branch8.com/posts/staff-augmentation-vs-managed-squad-apac-tech)


*Related reading:*[Apertus Open Foundation Model: Sovereign AI for APAC Teams](https://branch8.com/posts/apertus-open-foundation-model-sovereign-ai-apac)


There's a second, separate meaning of "Claude identity verification" worth clearing up before we build anything, because the search results mix them badly.


## Two different things called "Claude identity verification"


**1. Anthropic verifying** ***you*** **.** In 2025 Anthropic began rolling out identity and age verification for Claude consumer accounts, using Persona as the verification vendor, targeting suspected underage users, policy violators, and accounts in restricted jurisdictions ([The New Stack](https://thenewstack.io/) ). Anthropic's own help centre states verification data is used solely to confirm identity and meet legal and safety obligations ([Claude Help Center](https://support.claude.com/) ). If you're a developer on the API, this is mostly orthogonal — API authentication is separate from consumer identity verification, a point that dev.to and several Reddit threads have made repeatedly. What *does* affect developers is organisation-level verification for higher rate tiers and the Claude Cyber Verification Program for security-focused workloads.


**2. You using Claude to verify your customers.** That's the build in this guide — a Claude identity verification API integration that sits squarely inside AML/CFT obligations that differ between Singapore, Hong Kong, and Australia.


Do not let anyone sell you on "skip Claude KYC" proxy services that resell API access without verification. If you're a regulated entity in APAC, an unverified upstream vendor in your customer due diligence chain is an audit finding waiting to happen.


*Related reading:*[Looker vs Power BI: Retail Analytics APAC Comparison](https://branch8.com/posts/looker-vs-power-bi-retail-analytics-apac-comparison)


## Prerequisites


Before you write a line of code, have these in place:


- **An Anthropic Console account with a verified organisation** and an API key. Create keys at the Claude Console; store them in a secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, HashiCorp Vault), never in` .env` files committed to your repo.
- **A decision on data retention.** Anthropic's commercial terms state API inputs and outputs are not used to train models by default, with a standard retention window for trust and safety, according to Anthropic's own published terms ([Anthropic Privacy Center](https://www.anthropic.com/) ). For KYC payloads containing passport images, request **Zero Data Retention (ZDR)** on your organisation before processing a single real document. Check current terms at the Anthropic Privacy Center — this is the single most important prerequisite for a regulated workload.
- **A licensed IDV/biometric vendor** — Persona, Sumsub, Onfido, Jumio, or Trulioo. Claude does not perform liveness detection or 1:1 facial matching, and you should not try to make it.
- **An orchestration layer.** n8n (self-hosted, so documents never leave your VPC), Make, or your own service. For regulated workloads I strongly favour self-hosted n8n in your own cloud region — Singapore` ap-southeast-1` or Hong Kong` ap-east-1` .
- **A legal basis and privacy notice** aligned to Singapore's PDPA ([PDPC](https://www.pdpc.gov.sg/) ) and Hong Kong's PDPO ([PCPD](https://www.pcpd.org.hk/) ). According to the PDPC's 2022 amendment guidance, Singapore's PDPA financial penalty ceiling rose in October 2022 to up to 10% of annual turnover in Singapore for organisations with turnover above S$10 million. That number tends to focus the mind.
- **Python 3.11+ or Node 20+** , plus` curl` for testing.


*Related reading:*[Adobe Commerce to Shopify Plus Migration Playbook: 9 Phased Steps](https://branch8.com/posts/adobe-commerce-to-shopify-plus-migration-playbook)


One more: get your compliance officer in the room at design stage. Retro-fitting an audit trail onto a working pipeline is three times the work. I've watched teams try.

## Step 1: Verify your API access and model availability


Start with the dullest possible test — confirm the key works and the model responds.


```text
1  export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."    2
3  curl https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages \    4    -H "x-api-key: $ANTHROPIC_API_KEY" \    5    -H "anthropic-version: 2023-06-01" \    6    -H "content-type: application/json" \    7    -d '{    8      "model": "claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929",    9      "max_tokens": 64,    10      "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Reply with the single word: ready"}]    11    }'
```


Expected output:


```text
1  {     2      "id"  :     "msg_01XYZ..."  ,     3      "type"  :     "message"  ,     4      "role"  :     "assistant"  ,     5      "model"  :     "claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929"  ,     6      "content"  :     [  {  "type"  :     "text"  ,     "text"  :     "ready"  }  ]  ,     7      "stop_reason"  :     "end_turn"  ,     8      "usage"  :     {  "input_tokens"  :     16  ,     "output_tokens"  :     3  }     9   }
```


If you get a` 401` , your key is wrong or revoked. A` 429` means you've hit a rate limit for your organisation tier — relevant if you're batch-processing an onboarding backlog.


## Step 2: Replace long-lived API keys with workload identity federation


A static` sk-ant-` key sitting in an environment variable on a container that touches passport scans is the kind of thing that turns a minor incident into a notifiable breach. The Claude Platform now supports **Workload Identity Federation** : your workload presents a short-lived OIDC token from your own identity provider, and exchanges it for a short-lived Claude access token. No long-lived secret on the box.


The shape, using a GCP service account as the IdP:


```text
1  # 1. Get an OIDC token from your own IdP (GCP metadata server example)    2  OIDC_TOKEN=$(curl -s -H "Metadata-Flavor: Google" \    3    "http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1/instance/service-accounts/default/identity?audience=https://api.anthropic.com")    4
5  # 2. Exchange it for a short-lived Claude access token    6  #    (confirm the current endpoint + body in the Claude Platform docs)    7  curl -s "$CLAUDE_STS_ENDPOINT" \    8    -H "content-type: application/json" \    9    -d "{\"subject_token\":\"$OIDC_TOKEN\",\"workload_identity_pool\":\"$POOL_ID\"}"
```


Then call the Messages API with` Authorization: Bearer <access_token>` instead of` x-api-key` . Check the exact request shape in the[Claude Platform documentation](https://platform.claude.com/) before wiring it in — federation configuration is the kind of thing that changes.


Trade-off, honestly stated: federation adds setup complexity and an IdP dependency. For a 200-application-per-month onboarding flow, static keys rotated quarterly through a secrets manager may be proportionate. For anything processing identity documents at volume in a licensed entity, federation is worth the afternoon.

## Step 3: Build the document extraction call with enforced structure


This is the core of the integration. The mistake teams make is asking Claude for "a summary of this passport." You want a schema, every time, with no prose. Use tool definitions to force structured JSON output.


```text
1  import   base64  ,   json    2   from   anthropic   import   Anthropic    3
4  client   =   Anthropic  (  )      # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY     5
6  EXTRACT_TOOL   =     {     7        "name"  :     "record_identity_document"  ,     8        "description"  :     "Record fields extracted from a government-issued identity document."  ,     9        "input_schema"  :     {     10            "type"  :     "object"  ,     11            "properties"  :     {     12                "document_type"  :     {     13                    "type"  :     "string"  ,     14                    "enum"  :     [  "passport"  ,     "hkid"  ,     "sg_nric"  ,     "driver_licence"  ,     "other"  ,     "unreadable"  ]     15                }  ,     16                "issuing_jurisdiction"  :     {  "type"  :     "string"  ,     "description"  :     "ISO 3166-1 alpha-2, e.g. HK, SG, AU"  }  ,     17                "full_name_latin"  :     {  "type"  :     "string"  }  ,     18                "full_name_native"  :     {  "type"  :     "string"  ,     "description"  :     "Chinese characters if printed; empty if absent"  }  ,     19                "document_number"  :     {  "type"  :     "string"  }  ,     20                "date_of_birth"  :     {  "type"  :     "string"  ,     "description"  :     "YYYY-MM-DD, empty if not legible"  }  ,     21                "date_of_expiry"  :     {  "type"  :     "string"  ,     "description"  :     "YYYY-MM-DD, empty if not legible"  }  ,     22                "mrz_present"  :     {  "type"  :     "boolean"  }  ,     23                "tamper_indicators"  :     {     24                    "type"  :     "array"  ,     25                    "items"  :     {  "type"  :     "string"  }  ,     26                    "description"  :     "Visual anomalies observed: font mismatch, misaligned text, digital artefacts"     27                }  ,     28                "legibility_score"  :     {  "type"  :     "integer"  ,     "description"  :     "0-100 confidence the image is readable"  }  ,     29                "extraction_notes"  :     {  "type"  :     "string"  ,     "description"  :     "One sentence of rationale for the audit log"  }     30            }  ,     31            "required"  :     [  "document_type"  ,     "issuing_jurisdiction"  ,     "legibility_score"  ,     "extraction_notes"  ]     32        }     33   }     34
35  SYSTEM   =     (     36        "You extract fields from identity documents for a regulated financial institution. "     37        "Transcribe only what is visibly printed. Never infer, guess, or complete a partially "     38        "obscured field. If a field is not legible, return an empty string. You do not make "     39        "approve or reject decisions. Always call record_identity_document."     40   )     41
42   def     extract  (  image_bytes  :     bytes  ,   media_type  :     str     =     "image/jpeg"  )     -  >     dict  :     43      resp   =   client  .  messages  .  create  (     44          model  =  "claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929"  ,     45          max_tokens  =  1024  ,     46          temperature  =  0  ,     47          system  =  SYSTEM  ,     48          tools  =  [  EXTRACT_TOOL  ]  ,     49          tool_choice  =  {  "type"  :     "tool"  ,     "name"  :     "record_identity_document"  }  ,     50          messages  =  [  {     51                "role"  :     "user"  ,     52                "content"  :     [     53                    {  "type"  :     "image"  ,     "source"  :     {     54                        "type"  :     "base64"  ,     55                        "media_type"  :   media_type  ,     56                        "data"  :   base64  .  b64encode  (  image_bytes  )  .  decode  (  )     57                    }  }  ,     58                    {  "type"  :     "text"  ,     "text"  :     "Extract all legible fields from this document."  }     59                ]     60            }  ]     61        )     62        for   block   in   resp  .  content  :     63            if   block  .  type     ==     "tool_use"  :     64                return   block  .  input     65        raise   RuntimeError  (  "no tool_use block returned"  )
```


Copy-pasteable output for a clean Hong Kong passport scan:


```text
1  {     2      "document_type"  :     "passport"  ,     3      "issuing_jurisdiction"  :     "HK"  ,     4      "full_name_latin"  :     "CHAN TAI MAN"  ,     5      "full_name_native"  :     "陳大文"  ,     6      "document_number"  :     "K1234567"  ,     7      "date_of_birth"  :     "1988-03-14"  ,     8      "date_of_expiry"  :     "2031-07-02"  ,     9      "mrz_present"  :     true  ,     10      "tamper_indicators"  :     [  ]  ,     11      "legibility_score"  :     94  ,     12      "extraction_notes"  :     "All MRZ lines legible; printed fields match MRZ transliteration."     13   }
```


Three deliberate design choices there.` temperature=0` for determinism.` tool_choice` forced, so you never get a chatty paragraph where your parser expects JSON. And` extraction_notes` exists purely to give your compliance file a human-readable rationale — the thing an auditor asks for when they want to know why a record says what it says.


## Step 4: Cross-check against your IDV vendor, don't replace it


Here is where the architecture matters more than the prompt. Claude extracts. Persona (or Sumsub, or Onfido) does the regulated part: document authenticity, liveness, biometric match, PEP and sanctions screening. Your orchestrator compares the two and escalates on disagreement.


```text
1  from   datetime   import   date    2
3   def     reconcile  (  claude_fields  :     dict  ,   vendor_result  :     dict  )     -  >     dict  :     4      flags   =     [  ]     5
6        if   claude_fields  [  "legibility_score"  ]     <     70  :     7          flags  .  append  (  "LOW_LEGIBILITY"  )     8
9        if   claude_fields  .  get  (  "tamper_indicators"  )  :     10          flags  .  append  (  "VISUAL_TAMPER_SIGNAL"  )     11
12        def     norm  (  s  )  :     return     ""  .  join  (  ch   for   ch   in     (  s   or     ""  )  .  upper  (  )     if   ch  .  isalpha  (  )  )     13        if   norm  (  claude_fields  .  get  (  "full_name_latin"  )  )     !=   norm  (  vendor_result  .  get  (  "name"  )  )  :     14          flags  .  append  (  "NAME_MISMATCH"  )     15
16        if   claude_fields  .  get  (  "date_of_birth"  )     !=   vendor_result  .  get  (  "dob"  )  :     17          flags  .  append  (  "DOB_MISMATCH"  )     18
19      expiry   =   claude_fields  .  get  (  "date_of_expiry"  )     20        if   expiry   and   date  .  fromisoformat  (  expiry  )     <=   date  .  today  (  )  :     21          flags  .  append  (  "DOCUMENT_EXPIRED"  )     22
23        if   vendor_result  .  get  (  "liveness"  )     !=     "passed"  :     24          flags  .  append  (  "LIVENESS_FAIL"  )     25
26        return     {     27            "route"  :     "AUTO_CLEAR"     if     not   flags   else     "HUMAN_REVIEW"  ,     28            "flags"  :   flags  ,     29            "rationale"  :   claude_fields  .  get  (  "extraction_notes"  ,     ""  )     30        }
```


Output on a mismatch:


```text
1  {     2      "route"  :     "HUMAN_REVIEW"  ,     3      "flags"  :     [  "NAME_MISMATCH"  ,     "LOW_LEGIBILITY"  ]  ,     4      "rationale"  :     "Given name partially obscured by glare; surname legible."     5   }
```


Note what the model is *not* doing: it is not deciding. MAS Notice 626 and the associated AML/CFT guidelines permit non-face-to-face customer verification where the institution applies appropriate risk-mitigation measures, according to the Monetary Authority of Singapore's published notice ([MAS](https://www.mas.gov.sg/) ), and the HKMA has similarly supported remote onboarding of individual customers since its 2019 circulars, according to the HKMA's own circular guidance ([HKMA](https://www.hkma.gov.hk/) ). Both regimes put the accountability on the institution, not the vendor. An LLM output in your approval path is a control you must be able to explain, test, and override.

## Step 5: Orchestrate it in n8n with a human-in-the-loop branch


Self-hosted n8n is a good fit here because the document bytes stay inside your VPC, and the workflow is visible to a compliance reviewer who doesn't read Python. A minimal node sequence:


1. **Webhook** — receives the IDV vendor's` inquiry.completed` event.
2. **HTTP Request** — fetches the document image from your own object store (not the vendor's CDN, so you control retention).
3. **HTTP Request → Anthropic Messages API** — the Step 3 call.
4. **Code node** — the` reconcile()` logic.
5. **Switch node** —` AUTO_CLEAR` vs` HUMAN_REVIEW` .
6. **Postgres/Airtable node** — write the immutable audit record.
7. **Slack/Teams node** — notify the reviewer queue with flags and rationale.


The webhook verification step is non-negotiable:


```text
1  // n8n Code node: verify the IDV provider's webhook signature before anything else     2   const   crypto   =     require  (  'crypto'  )  ;     3   const   raw   =   $input  .  first  (  )  .  json  .  rawBody  ;     4   const   received   =   $input  .  first  (  )  .  json  .  headers  [  'persona-signature'  ]  ;     5
6   const   expected   =   crypto    7      .  createHmac  (  'sha256'  ,   $env  .  IDV_WEBHOOK_SECRET  )     8      .  update  (  raw  )     9      .  digest  (  'hex'  )  ;     10
11   if     (  !  crypto  .  timingSafeEqual  (  Buffer  .  from  (  expected  )  ,     Buffer  .  from  (  received  )  )  )     {     12      throw     new     Error  (  'Webhook signature mismatch — dropping payload'  )  ;     13   }     14   return   $input  .  all  (  )  ;
```


A practical detail from building this kind of pipeline with a Greater China retail group handling cross-border customer registrations: set your n8n execution data pruning aggressively (` EXECUTIONS_DATA_MAX_AGE` ,` EXECUTIONS_DATA_PRUNE=true` ). By default, orchestrators cheerfully store the full payload of every run — including base64 passport images — in their own database, according to n8n's own hosting and self-deployment documentation ([n8n Docs](https://docs.n8n.io/) ). That's a copy of your most sensitive data in a system nobody listed on the data inventory.


```text
1  # docker-compose env for self-hosted n8n handling PII    2  EXECUTIONS_DATA_PRUNE=true    3  EXECUTIONS_DATA_MAX_AGE=72          # hours    4  EXECUTIONS_DATA_SAVE_ON_SUCCESS=none    5  N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY=${VAULT_N8N_KEY}
```


## Step 6: Redact, log, and make it auditable


Two logs, different lifetimes. The **operational log** holds full extracted fields and lives as long as your AML record-keeping obligation requires — five years from the end of the business relationship under Singapore's AML/CFT notices and Hong Kong's AMLO. The **debug log** holds model latency, token counts, model version, and flags, with every PII field masked.


```text
1  import   re  ,   hashlib    2
3  SENSITIVE   =     (  "document_number"  ,     "date_of_birth"  ,     "full_name_latin"  ,     "full_name_native"  )     4
5   def     redact_for_telemetry  (  fields  :     dict  )     -  >     dict  :     6      out   =     dict  (  fields  )     7        for   k   in   SENSITIVE  :     8            if   out  .  get  (  k  )  :     9              out  [  k  ]     =     "sha256:"     +   hashlib  .  sha256  (  out  [  k  ]  .  encode  (  )  )  .  hexdigest  (  )  [  :  12  ]     10        return   out
```


Pin the model version in your audit record. When Anthropic ships a new Sonnet, your extraction behaviour can shift, and "which model made this extraction on 14 March" is a question you want a one-line answer to. Log` model` ,` prompt_version` ,` tool_schema_version` , and` usage` on every call.

## Step 7: Evaluate before you ship — with regional documents


Most teams test with US passports and an Australian driver licence, then deploy into a market where half the uploads are a photo of a Hong Kong ID card taken at an angle under fluorescent light, or a Vietnamese CCCD, or an Indonesian KTP with a laminate reflection across the NIK.


Build a golden set of 200–400 real-shape documents (synthetic or consented), spanning:


- HKID, Singapore NRIC/FIN, Malaysian MyKad, Indonesian KTP, Philippine PhilID, Vietnamese CCCD, Taiwan ID
- Chinese-character names, including traditional and simplified
- Glare, 15–30° rotation, partial crop, low resolution, screenshot-of-a-screen


Measure field-level exact-match accuracy and, more importantly, **the rate at which the model returns a confident value that is wrong** . Silent errors are the dangerous failure mode; a blank field routes to a human, a wrong field routes to an account.


```text
1  python eval.py --dataset golden_apac_v3.jsonl \    2    --model claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929 \    3    --metrics exact_match,silent_error_rate,escalation_rate
```


Set an escalation threshold your operations team can actually staff. If 35% of applications route to human review, you need to know that before you promise the business a 4-hour SLA.


## Where regional compliance actually bites


Three things that catch APAC teams:


**Cross-border transfer.** Sending a Singapore customer's NRIC image to a US-hosted inference endpoint is a transfer. Under the PDPA Transfer Limitation Obligation you need comparable protection in place; Hong Kong's PDPO section 33 remains uncommenced but the PCPD's guidance on cross-border transfers still sets the expectation. Document the transfer, the safeguards, and the ZDR arrangement.


**Automated decision-making.** Keep a human in the loop on adverse outcomes. If you operate into the EU as well, GDPR Article 22 restricts solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects, and account rejection qualifies, according to the European Data Protection Board's guidance on automated decision-making ([EDPB](https://edpb.europa.eu/) ).


**Vendor concentration.** Your regulator will ask what happens if Anthropic's API is unavailable mid-onboarding. Have a documented fallback: queue to manual review, don't fail the application.

## What to do next


Run it in shadow mode first. Point the Claude identity verification API integration at live traffic, write its output to a separate table, and let your analysts keep working as they always have. After three or four weeks you'll have a real comparison between model extraction and human extraction on *your* document mix — which is the only dataset that matters for the go/no-go call. Then enable auto-clear for your lowest-risk segment only, and widen from there.


Honest assessment of who this is *not* for. If you onboard fewer than roughly 100 customers a month, the engineering, evaluation, and compliance documentation cost will exceed what you save on analyst hours — buy an all-in-one IDV platform instead. If you're in a jurisdiction where your regulator has not yet published a position on AI in CDD workflows, expect to spend more time in written correspondence than in code. And if your compliance team isn't resourced to own and periodically re-test a model-based control, don't build one; an unmonitored automated control is worse than a slow manual one, because it fails quietly.


For everyone else — teams running cross-border onboarding across Hong Kong, Singapore, and Southeast Asia, where document variety is the actual bottleneck — a well-scoped Claude identity verification API integration moves the human effort from transcription to judgement. That's the right trade.
